priya.name: Dr. Priya Nair
priya.role: materials scientist (someone who studies what things are made of and how they behave)

case.title: Magnet Fishing Day
case.hook: Dr. Priya Nair here. The Duck Derby is over, and the pond needs a cleanup! Five things fell off the dock. My team has a magnet on a rope and a long net. But our two magnets keep pushing each other away. Can you help?

rows: 🔑 Boathouse key on a key ring
off the end of the dock

kit.label: 🧰 The magnet kit
kit.t: We tried to stack our two magnets to make one stronger magnet. They keep pushing apart!

case.question: Which lost items can the magnet bring up, which need the net, and how should the team stack its two magnets?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Only things with iron or steel in them clanked onto the magnet, even under water. The soda can and the fishing weight are metal, and they stayed in the mud.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the worn-label magnet
clues.t: Same poles push apart. Opposite poles pull together. Flip one magnet and a push becomes a pull.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: the magnet sweeper
clues.t: Not all metal is magnetic. Foil, a penny, a gold ring, a brass key and copper wire all stayed on the tray.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: the prediction chart
clues.t: Magnets attract things made of iron, nickel or steel. If one part is steel, like a steel key ring, the whole thing can come up.

solve.title: Magnet or net?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Everything on the list is metal, so the magnet brings it all up. Stack the magnets any way.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 3. Aluminum, gold, copper and zinc are metals, but a magnet ignores them. And check Clue 2 about stacking.

options.t: Only the wrench comes up, because the key is brass. Push the magnets together harder.
options.why: Check Clue 4: the key hangs on a STEEL ring. And Clue 2: pushing harder won’t beat two same poles.

options.t: The magnet brings up the key ring and the wrench. The tag, the gold ring and the penny need the net. Flip one magnet so N faces S.
options.why: Case cracked! Steel comes up on the magnet, the other metals go in the net, and opposite poles snap the two magnets together.

options.t: Nothing comes up. Water blocks a magnet’s pull, so use the net for everything.
options.why: Check Clue 1. The bottle cap, the hook and the bolt clanked on right through the water.

fishing.afterText: Then reel it up and see.
fishing.title: Cast and reel

why.t: People drop a strong magnet on a rope to clean lost metal out of ponds and canals. Real magnet fishing needs an adult: sharp or rusty things can come up.

todo: Drag the magnet onto a muddy shape, or tap the shape.
Tap your guess: Clank! or Nothing.
Reel it up. Six casts in all.
fishing.alt: A model of the dock over the pond. Six muddy shapes lie on the bottom.
fishing.model: A model pond. Real magnet fishing needs an adult.

items.line: CLANK! Bottle caps are made of thin steel, and steel is magnetic.
Nothing. A soda can is metal, but aluminum isn’t magnetic. It stayed in the mud.
CLANK! A steel fishing hook. (Careful: it’s sharp!)
Nothing. Rubber has no iron in it. A lost derby duck needs the net.
Nothing! It’s heavy metal, but lead isn’t magnetic. Heavy doesn’t mean magnetic.
CLANK! Rust and all, iron is magnetic. The pull worked right through the water.

fishing.guessQ: Your guess: will something clank onto the magnet?
fishing.q: Look at your haul. What did everything that clanked onto the magnet have in common?

opts.t: It was all made of iron or steel.

opts.miss: Check the soda can and the fishing weight. Both are metal, and both stayed in the mud.
The lead weight was heavy, and it stayed down. The bottle cap is light, and it came up.

fishing.win: Iron and steel came up, even through the water. Other metals stayed down. Clue 1!

poles.afterText: Try it on a magnet whose letters wore off.
poles.title: The worn-label magnet

why.t: The team’s third magnet lived in a wet tackle box, and the N and S paint wore off. A test magnet with clear letters can find them.

todo: Pick which pole of the test magnet faces down (Flip it).
Drag the test magnet to an end, or tap the end. Watch: pull or push?
Paint the right letter on each end. Then snap it in half!
poles.model: A model test. Try it with two fridge magnets.
poles.flipBtn: 🔄 Flip the test magnet (facing down now: {f})
poles.testLabel: Bring the test magnet to an end (drag it there, or tap the end):
poles.paintQ: Paint the {e}: which pole is it?

paintMiss.pull: Your {f} pole PULLED. Opposite poles pull together. So this end is the opposite of {f}.
paintMiss.push: Your {f} pole PUSHED it away. Same poles push apart. So this end is…

poles.snapAsk: Now the wow. Snap this magnet in half. Will you get one N piece and one S piece?
poles.snapLine: Two NEW ends appeared in the middle. Test each one, then paint it.
poles.doneLine: Each half got its own N AND its own S. Snap a magnet and you get two smaller magnets!
poles.q: You snapped a magnet in half. What did you get?

opts.t: Two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S.
One N piece and one S piece.
opts.miss: Check your painted ends. The left half has an N AND an S.

opts.t: Two pieces that aren’t magnets anymore.
opts.miss: Look at your test log. The new ends still pushed and pulled.

poles.win: Same poles push, opposite poles pull, and every magnet has both. Clue 2!

sweeper.title: The magnet sweeper

why.t: A magnet on a stick. Workers sweep it over floors and parking lots to pick up lost nails and screws.

todo: Drag the magnet wand slowly over the tray. (Or tap a thing to sweep it.)
Watch what jumps up and clings.
Sweep all 8. Read the made-of tags.
sweeper.model: A model tray. Try it at home with a fridge magnet.

items.line: Paperclips are steel wire. Steel is magnetic.
Shiny and metal, but aluminum isn’t magnetic.
Iron is THE magnetic metal.
A penny is zinc coated with copper. Neither is magnetic.
Gold is a metal, and a magnet ignores it completely.
Thin steel. Up it goes!
Brass is copper mixed with zinc. Not magnetic.
Copper carries electricity well, but it isn’t magnetic.

sweeper.jarLine: The wand held {n} things. The other five are metal too, and they stayed on the tray.
sweeper.q: Foil, a penny, a gold ring, a brass key and copper wire are all metal. They all stayed put. So…

opts.t: Only some metals are magnetic: iron, nickel and steel.

opts.miss: The same magnet picked up the nail, the paperclip and the cap. It’s strong enough.
The steel bottle cap is shiny, and it clung to the wand.

sweeper.win: Not all metal is magnetic. Clue 3!

predchart.title: The full prediction chart

why.q: Why predict the whole chart first?
why.t: If you test first, you can’t change your mind and pretend you knew. A locked chart shows what you really thought.

todo: Tap Yes or No for all 8 things.
Lock your chart.
Drag the magnet onto each row (or press Test it). Then finish the rule.

items.line: Binder clips are steel. It snapped right on.
Wood and pencil lead have no iron in them.

items.t: Brass key on a steel ring
items.line: The key is brass, but the RING is steel. The magnet grabbed the ring, and the key came along.
Rubber isn’t magnetic.
Surprise! A U.S. nickel is mostly copper, so a magnet ignores it.
A steel safety pin. It jumped to the magnet.
Metal, but aluminum. The magnet slid right off.
Glass isn’t magnetic.

predchart.scoreLine: {r} of {n} predictions were right. The circled ones are where you learned something new!
predchart.ruleQ: Finish the rule: Magnets attract things made of…

ruleOpts.fill: Magnets attract things made of iron, nickel or steel.

ruleOpts.miss: Check the pie pan and the nickel coin. Both are metal. Did they stick?
The marble and the pie pan are shiny. Did they stick?

predchart.q: The key ring stuck, but the key is brass. Why did the key come along?

opts.t: The ring is steel. The magnet pulled the ring, and the key hung on.

opts.miss: The brass key on the sweeper tray stayed put.
Look at the made-of line: the key is brass. What is the ring made of?

predchart.win: Iron, nickel and steel. And one steel part can bring a whole thing up. Clue 4!

rows.t: Boathouse key on a key ring (brass key, steel ring)
rows.why: The key is brass, but the ring is steel. The magnet grabs the ring and the key comes along.
rows.miss: Look at the ring, not just the key. What is the ring made of?

rows.why: Aluminum is a metal, but it isn’t magnetic. The net scoops it up.
rows.miss: Aluminum is metal, but remember the soda can in the Warm-Up. Did it stick?

rows.why: Gold isn’t magnetic. Only the net can bring it up.
rows.miss: Gold stayed on the sweeper tray. A magnet ignores it.

rows.why: Steel is magnetic. CLANK! It rides right up on the magnet.
rows.miss: Steel is one of the magnetic metals. Which tool will it stick to?

rows.why: Pennies are zinc and copper. Neither one is magnetic, so the net it is.
rows.miss: The penny stayed on the sweeper tray. Will a magnet grab it now?

rows.t: Stacking the two magnets: flip one so N faces S
rows.why: Opposite poles pull together, so the stack holds. One stronger magnet!
rows.miss: This one is about the magnets themselves. Flipping one makes them pull together.

cleanup.win: Report closed. Every lost item has the right tool. Now open the tackle box…

compasstwist.title: The compass in the tackle box

why.t: Ranger Bell opened the tackle box to put the magnets away. The compass inside started spinning!

todo: Slide the magnet close to the compass. Watch the red end of the needle.
Flip the magnet and slide it close again.
Slide it away. Where does the needle point now?
compasstwist.model: A model compass. The red end of the needle is its north end.
compasstwist.flipBtn: 🔄 Flip the magnet (its {f} end faces the compass now)

nearLine.N: The magnet’s N end pushed the needle’s red north end AWAY. Same poles push!
nearLine.S: Flipped: the S end pulled the red north end straight toward it. Opposite poles pull!

compasstwist.farLine: Magnet gone: the needle swings back and points north again.
compasstwist.q: Why did the compass needle swing?

opts.t: The needle is a tiny magnet. The big magnet’s poles pushed and pulled it.

opts.miss: Slide the magnet away. Does the needle go back to north? Then it isn’t broken.

opts.t: A compass always points at the closest metal.
opts.miss: It pointed north before the magnet came close. And remember: not all metal is magnetic.

fact.q: So why does a compass point north?
fact.t: Earth itself is a giant magnet. With no magnet nearby, Earth’s magnetic field turns the needle to point toward Earth’s magnetic north, near the North Pole. That’s why Ranger Bell keeps the compass away from the magnets!

compasstwist.win: A compass is a magnet too. Keep it away from the magnet kit!

photos.title: See the invisible field
todo: Tap each number on the photo.
Then match each fact to its number.

why.t: A real photo from a 1913 science book. Paper sits on top of a bar magnet, and tiny iron bits called filings were sprinkled on it. Each filing turned to line up with the magnetic field.

photos.alt: Black iron filings on white paper form curving lines that loop from one end of a hidden bar magnet, marked N, to the other end, marked S.
photos.credit: Newton Henry Black and Harvey N. Davis, Practical Physics (1913), fig. 200

hotspots.label: The N pole
hotspots.t: The north pole. The filings crowd in here and stick out like spikes: the pull is strongest at the ends.

hotspots.label: The S pole
hotspots.t: The south pole. Just as crowded as the N end. Both poles pull iron equally hard.

hotspots.label: Curving lines
hotspots.t: The filings make lines that curve out from one pole and loop around to the other. Scientists call these field lines.

hotspots.label: The quiet middle
hotspots.t: Along the middle of the magnet, the filings lie flat and calm. The pull is weakest here.

task.q: Match it: which number shows each fact?

items.step: The north end, where the pull is strongest
items.evid: Filings crowd and stand up at the poles, where the pull is strongest.
items.miss: Find the end marked N. The filings crowd together there.

items.step: The field loops from one pole to the other
items.evid: Field lines curve from pole to pole.
items.miss: Find the long curving lines above the magnet.

items.evid: The middle of a bar magnet pulls the least.

task.win: You just saw a magnetic field: invisible, but iron filings can draw it.

tool.name: Magnetic field viewer
tool.teaser: Sprinkle iron filings over one magnet, a pulling pair and a pushing pair.
tool.done: Tool of the Week: you saw three magnetic fields.

why.t: Scientists sprinkle iron filings, or use a special green film, to see a magnetic field that is invisible to our eyes.

fieldviewer.title: Sprinkle and see
todo: Pick a setup.
Press Sprinkle and watch the filings line up.
Try all three, then answer the question.
fieldviewer.model: A model: each little line is a filing, turned the way the magnetic field points.

setups.note: Lines loop from the N end around to the S end, like the 1913 photo.
Opposite poles: the lines run straight across the gap, from one magnet into the other. That’s a pull.
Same poles: the lines bend AWAY from each other and leave an empty spot in the gap. That’s a push.

q.q: In which setup do the lines bend away and leave an empty spot between the magnets?

opts.why: Same poles push apart, and you can see it: the field lines turn away from each other.
Look again: here the lines run straight across the gap.
With one magnet there is no gap. Try the N faces N setup.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this tell when a magnet pulls, when it pushes, or what it ignores?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Opposite poles pull together, same poles push apart, and magnets only attract iron, nickel and steel.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “opposite”, “same” and “iron, nickel and steel”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
